title: Winning direct orders back from delivery apps

description: Bring back direct orders with better phone handling, simple promos, and a smoother ordering flow. Reduce reliance on third-party apps.
question: How do I win direct orders back from third-party apps for my restaurant?
answer: Start by making phone ordering easier than the apps: answer faster, quote clearly, and take pickup or delivery orders from your live menu without making guests wait. Then give customers a reason to call direct, such as faster help, accurate menu answers, and simple pickup instructions. Tools like ROAL can help by answering calls, taking orders, and sending clean tickets to the kitchen.
summary: You will learn how to make phone ordering easier, cheaper, and more appealing than delivery apps.
intro:
Third-party apps can be useful for getting found, but they often take a big bite out of each order. If you want more direct orders restaurant owners can keep for themselves, the fix is usually not one big marketing stunt. It is making the phone the easiest way to order.

That means faster answers, fewer missed calls, clear menu info, and a smooth handoff to the kitchen. It also means giving people a small reason to call you directly instead of paying app fees. ROAL is built for that: it answers the phone, takes pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

sections.h2: Why are direct orders worth fighting for?
sections.body:
Direct orders matter because they usually cost less than app orders. Third-party delivery apps commonly charge restaurants roughly 15-30% commission per order, and that can add up fast on a $25 or $40 ticket. With direct orders, you keep more of the sale and you also get the caller’s name and number for future repeat business.

Here is a simple way to look at it:

| Example order | App commission at 15% | App commission at 30% |
|---|---:|---:|
| $25 | $3.75 | $7.50 |
| $40 | $6.00 | $12.00 |

Plug in your own average order. If you take a lot of pickup orders, even a few extra direct calls a day can matter more than a small jump in app volume. The point is not to quit apps overnight. The point is to keep the orders you can control.

A good owner rule is simple: every caller should get an easy path to order direct. If they have to wait on hold, repeat themselves, or hear “call back later,” they will go elsewhere. That is where a phone host like [ROAL](/about) can help by answering the phone, quoting the order back, and sending the ticket straight to the kitchen.

sections.h2: What should you fix on the phone first?
sections.body:
Most restaurants lose direct orders on the phone before the customer ever reaches the menu. The problem is usually not the food. It is the wait, the confusion, or the missed call.

Start with this short checklist:
- Answer quickly, especially during rushes.
- Know your hours, address, parking, and best-selling items.
- Make pickup and delivery ordering easy to hear and repeat.
- Tell the caller the ready time before the call ends.
- Give a clean path for allergies, catering, and manager requests.

A simple phone script can help your team stay consistent:
"Thanks for calling. We can take your order now for pickup or delivery. I’ll repeat it back, give you the ready time, and send it to the kitchen."

That script does three useful things. It tells the caller they can order now, it sets a clear process, and it gives confidence. If you use ROAL, it can handle this flow from your live menu and even speak the caller’s language. It also will not offer items marked sold out, which avoids the awkward back-and-forth that often kills a direct order.

sections.h2: How do you make direct ordering easier than an app?
sections.body:
To win direct orders back, your phone experience has to feel easier than opening an app and waiting on a driver estimate. That does not mean fancy tech. It means fewer steps and clearer answers.

Use this comparison as a practical target:

| Step | Delivery app | Direct phone order goal |
|---|---|---|
| Find the menu | Open app, browse listings | Hear the menu or ask for items fast |
| Ask a question | Search the app or message support | Get an answer on the same call |
| Place order | Tap through screens | Speak one time, confirm once |
| Get ready time | App estimate | Restaurant gives a ready time directly |

Here is a concrete example. Say a customer wants two slices, a salad, and a soda. On the phone, the order should sound like this:
"Two slices, one salad, and one soda. Any dressing on the side? Great. Your total is $28, and it will be ready in about 20 minutes."

That feels fast. It also feels personal. If your team is too busy to do that during rush hour, an AI phone host can help. ROAL reads the live menu, takes items, sizes, modifiers, and notes, then confirms the order back before sending it to the kitchen screen. That is the kind of smooth experience that can bring direct callers back.

sections.h2: What offer or message should you use to pull people away from apps?
sections.body:
You do not need a huge discount to pull some customers back. Often, a cleaner promise works better than a coupon. People call direct when they expect faster help, fewer mistakes, and less hassle.

Try one of these messages on your menu, receipts, website, or social posts:
- "Order direct by phone for quick pickup help and menu questions."
- "Call us to place your order and get a ready time before you hang up."
- "Need substitutions or allergy questions? Call us directly."

If you want to make the switch more measurable, use a simple example:
- Say your average direct order is $30.
- Say one app order would cost you 20% in commission, or $6.
- If a caller switches to direct, you may keep that $6 inside the business instead of sending it away.

You can also use direct ordering for customers who want a human answer, not another checkout screen. That matters for older regulars, large family orders, and people with special requests. A phone host can help there because it can answer hours, address, parking, and menu questions while the caller is still interested. For common menu and ordering questions, see [menu, hours and allergen questions](/use-cases/menu-questions).

sections.h2: How can call forwarding and coverage protect more direct orders?
sections.body:
A lot of direct orders are lost because the phone rings unanswered at the worst possible moment. Lunch rush, dinner rush, one person in the back, and suddenly the caller hangs up. That is why forwarding matters.

Most owners should know the basic setup options, but always confirm with your carrier or phone system and test it with a real call. On many landlines and some carriers, dial *72 then the forwarding number to forward all calls, and *73 to turn it off. On some GSM mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off; **61*number# forwards unanswered calls and **67*number# forwards busy calls. Verizon Wireless uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding. Business VoIP systems usually set forwarding in the web portal.

Use this checklist before you go live:
1. Test forwarding during a quiet hour.
2. Call from a mobile phone and make sure it rings where you expect.
3. Check that the caller can still place an order normally.
4. Make sure staff know when forwarding is on and off.

ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically once the owner claims the host, and the restaurant can forward its existing number to it. That means you can send all calls, or only busy and unanswered calls, depending on your setup. The restaurant keeps its own number, and forwarding can be turned off any time.

sections.h2: How do you turn callers into repeat direct customers?
sections.body:
Winning direct orders back is not only about the first call. It is about making the second call easier. If a customer had a good phone experience, they are more likely to use the same number again.

The best repeat-order habits are simple:
- Save the customer’s name and number when the order is taken.
- Give a clear ready time every time.
- Keep the kitchen ticket clean so the order comes out right.
- Answer questions once, then keep that answer for next time.

Here is a practical repeat-order routine you can use:
- Customer calls for a pickup order.
- The host confirms items, sizes, modifiers, and notes.
- The host repeats the order back.
- The kitchen gets a clean ticket.
- Next time, the caller already knows the process is easy.

ROAL includes call history with transcripts and recordings, plus a menu editor, hours, FAQs, upsell suggestions, and multi-location menus in the dashboard. If the host cannot answer a question, it goes to an inbox. You answer it once, and the host knows it from then on. That helps the phone get better over time without making the customer wait.

sections.h2: What should you measure this week?
sections.body:
You do not need a complicated marketing plan to start. You need a few numbers you can check by hand. Pick one week and track what happens on the phone.

Use this simple scorecard:

| Metric | What to write down |
|---|---|
| Calls answered | How many calls got a live or hosted answer |
| Direct orders taken | How many orders were placed by phone |
| Missed calls | How many rang out or went to voicemail |
| Common questions | Hours, address, parking, menu items |
| Problem calls | Allergy, catering, complaint, manager requests |

Then ask one question: where are callers getting stuck? If the problem is hours and address questions, fix your public info. If the problem is slow ordering, tighten your script. If the problem is missed calls, set up forwarding or use an AI phone host.

If you want a simple place to start, [build a free test host from your website](/try). You can paste your restaurant website, Google Maps link, or name and city, then test-call it in the browser before deciding whether to go live.

takeaways: Direct orders usually cost less than delivery app orders.
The fastest win is answering the phone clearly and consistently.
A clean order flow, clear ready times, and fewer missed calls bring callers back.
ROAL can take orders from your live menu and send them to the kitchen.
Track calls, missed calls, and problem questions before you change everything.

faq.q: How do I get more direct orders instead of delivery app orders?
faq.a: Make the phone easier and faster than the app. Answer calls quickly, quote a ready time, and keep menu questions simple to resolve. A clear phone path, plus a small message like "call direct for pickup help," can move more customers back to you.

faq.q: Is it cheaper to take direct orders by phone than through apps?
faq.a: Often, yes. Third-party delivery apps commonly charge roughly 15-30% commission per order, while direct phone orders do not carry that same commission. Your own costs depend on your phone setup and staffing, so compare those against your average order size.

faq.q: What if my staff is too busy to answer every call?
faq.a: That is a common problem during lunch and dinner rushes. You can forward calls to an AI phone host or route unanswered and busy calls so more callers still get an answer. If a call is too complex, it can be handed to staff with a summary.

faq.q: Can ROAL take payment over the phone?
faq.a: No. ROAL does not take card numbers over the phone. Payment happens at pickup or however the restaurant already takes it, and the host focuses on taking the order, confirming it, and sending a clean ticket to the kitchen.
